title: הבטון שבונה את עצמו מחדש כבר אלפיים שנה
summary: Roman self-healing concrete: Herod poured concrete into the sea at Caesarea (22–15 BCE, 10 km from Zikhron Yaakov) using ~24,000 m³ of Puteoli pozzolana (52,000 t ≈ 130 shiploads) that sets under water (Vitruvius 1:2); the white lime clasts long dismissed as bad mixing are, per MIT's 2023 Science Advances paper (Masic, Seymour), quicklime from hot mixing (55–60°C above ambient) — brittle, porous calcium reservoirs: water in a crack dissolves them and the calcium recrystallises as calcite, sealing a 0.5 mm crack within weeks (control never healed); Jackson 2017: seawater grows Al-tobermorite/phillipsite so marine Roman concrete strengthens; modern concrete fails because rebar rust expands and widens cracks (50–100 yr); the Caesarea harbour itself sank (fault, tsunami), the concrete held.
reviewer_verdict: PASS (2 rounds) — nits left: reviewer estimates ~35–45 min vs the 30-min tag (same word counts as #19/#20); canvas label plates touch the edges by a few px at 640-unit scale; series-wide 'שלחו לאבא' strings
